name: list=
summary: True when every list given is the same as every other, element by element, under the equality you supply.
explanation: equal? compares two lists using its own fixed idea of sameness, recursively, all the way down. list= lets you say what sameness means, and lets you ask about any number of lists at once. That first freedom is the important one: two price lists are the same if they agree to the cent, two word lists are the same ignoring case, two readings are the same within tolerance -- and none of those are equal?. The second freedom removes a pattern you would otherwise write by hand, since (and (list= e a b) (list= e b c)) is what you would have typed and it is one call instead. The verb compares pairwise down the chain and stops at the first disagreement, so a mismatch in the first two lists costs nothing to discover. With zero or one list it is vacuously true, which sounds like a technicality until you are folding over a collection that might have one element in it.

examples.note: (#t #f) -- with equal? it is the ordinary list comparison you already expect.

examples.code:
(define (close? a b) (< (abs (- a b)) 0.5))
(display (list 'tolerant (list= close? '(1.0 2.0) '(1.2 1.9))
               'strict (list= equal? '(1.0 2.0) '(1.2 1.9))
               'three (list= close? '(1.0) '(1.1) '(0.9))))
(newline)
examples.note: (tolerant #t strict #f three #t) -- the equality is a parameter, so approximate sameness is just a different argument.

examples.code:
(define (same-shape? a b) (eq? (even? a) (even? b)))
(display (list 'agree (list= same-shape? '(2 4 6) '(8 10 12) '(0 2 4))
               'differ (list= same-shape? '(2 4) '(2 5))
               'lengths (list= same-shape? '(2 4) '(2 4 6))
               'vacuous (list= same-shape? '(9))))
(newline)
examples.note: (agree #t differ #f lengths #f vacuous #t) -- unequal lengths are never equal, and a single list is trivially equal to itself.

caveats: The equality predicate comes FIRST, before any list. Passing the lists first is the usual mistake and it fails as a bad procedure call.
With zero or one list the answer is #t. That is vacuous truth, not a claim about the contents, and it matters when the argument count is computed.
Lists of different lengths are never list=, whatever the predicate says about the elements they share.
The comparison is one level deep -- your predicate is called on ELEMENTS. It does not recurse into sublists unless your predicate does.
It compares pairwise and short-circuits, so a predicate with side effects will not be called on every pair of every list once a mismatch is found.
The predicate should be an equivalence -- reflexive, symmetric, transitive. Handing it something asymmetric like < produces an answer, but not a meaningful one.
usecases: Comparing numeric records within a tolerance instead of exactly.
Case-insensitive or normalised comparison of lists of strings or symbols.
Checking that several parallel results all agree, without chaining two-way comparisons.

learn.concept: Sameness is a parameter, not a property -- and once it is a parameter, comparison generalises to as many things as you like at once.
learn.progression: Compare two lists with equal? and be satisfied. Then compare two lists of floating-point measurements and watch equal? say no about numbers you consider the same. Write your own tolerance comparison, then discover you also want it for three lists, and list= is already both of those things.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (cents= a b) (= (round (* 100 a)) (round (* 100 b))))
(define (invoices-agree? . sheets) (apply list= cents= sheets))
(display (list 'match (invoices-agree? '(10.00 5.25) '(10.001 5.2499))
               'off-by-a-cent (invoices-agree? '(10.00 5.25) '(10.00 5.26))
               'three-way (invoices-agree? '(1.5) '(1.499) '(1.5004))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (congruent-mod-7? a b) (= (modulo a 7) (modulo b 7)))
(define (same-residues? . rows) (apply list= congruent-mod-7? rows))
(display (list 'same (same-residues? '(1 2 3) '(8 9 10))
               'shifted (same-residues? '(1 2 3) '(8 9 11))
               'four (same-residues? '(0) '(7) '(14) '(21))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define (calls-counted pred)
  (let ((n 0))
    (list (lambda (a b) (set! n (+ n 1)) (pred a b)) (lambda () n))))
(define c1 (calls-counted =))
(define c2 (calls-counted =))
(define r1 (list= (car c1) '(1 9 9 9) '(2 9 9 9)))
(define r2 (list= (car c2) '(1 2 3 4) '(1 2 3 4)))
(display (list 'mismatch r1 'calls ((cadr c1)) 'match r2 'calls ((cadr c2))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A reconciliation job must decide whether two or three invoice sheets say the same thing, where the amounts came from different systems and round differently. Candidates: list= with a cents predicate (the tolerance is stated once, the number of sheets is whatever arrived, and it short-circuits), equal? (compares the floating-point values exactly and reports a mismatch that is not real), (every cents= a b) (correct for two sheets, but it does not check lengths and does not extend to three), sorting and comparing (destroys the positional correspondence that makes the comparison meaningful), a hand-written recursive walk (this is exactly list= re-typed, with a fresh chance to get the length case wrong). list= is the pick because the equality is the thing that varies and it is the thing list= takes as an argument.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: invoice reconciliation to the cent, run on sheets that agree after rounding, sheets that differ by a real cent, and three sheets at once. math: residue comparison mod 7, where 1 and 8 are the same number for the purpose at hand, across a matching pair, a mismatching one, and four lists in a single call. cs: instrumenting the predicate to count calls, which shows the comparison stopping at the first disagreement rather than finishing the list.
row-2-audit.meta: The cs program is the only one that observes list= rather than using it. Counting predicate calls is how you show short-circuiting exists at all, since the return value of a mismatched comparison looks identical whether it stopped early or not.
row-2-audit.eng: Money compared as floating point is a bug waiting for a rounding boundary. Compare the integer cents and the question becomes exact again.
row-2-audit.math: Congruence mod n is an equivalence relation, so it is a legitimate argument to list=. Feeding it a relation that is not an equivalence produces a result with no meaning attached.
row-2-audit.cs: Short-circuiting is observable only through side effects. If your predicate is pure -- and it should be -- the optimisation is invisible and free.

row-3-dimension.setup: Asking whether several sequences say the same thing, under a notion of sameness you choose.

rungs.domain: three laboratory instruments reporting the same sample, each with its own precision
rungs.code:
(define (within tol) (lambda (a b) (<= (abs (- a b)) tol)))
(define run-a '(4.01 7.98 2.50))
(define run-b '(4.00 8.02 2.49))
(define run-c '(4.03 7.95 2.52))
(define (agree-at tol) (list= (within tol) run-a run-b run-c))
(display (map (lambda (t) (list t (agree-at t))) '(0.01 0.05 0.10)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a differential tester checking that three implementations of the same routine produce matching output
rungs.code:
(define (impl-a xs) (map (lambda (n) (* n n)) xs))
(define (impl-b xs) (map (lambda (n) (* n n)) (reverse (reverse xs))))
(define (impl-c xs) (map (lambda (n) (+ (* n n) (if (> n 3) 1 0))) xs))
(define (differential inputs)
  (let loop ((r inputs) (bad '()))
    (cond ((null? r) (if (null? bad) 'all-agree (list 'diverged-on (reverse bad))))
          ((list= = (impl-a (car r)) (impl-b (car r)) (impl-c (car r))) (loop (cdr r) bad))
          (else (loop (cdr r) (cons (car r) bad))))))
(display (list 'small (differential '((1 2) (0) (3 2)))
               'wide (differential '((1 2) (4 5) (3)))))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers it is a four-case sanity check and the tolerance question does not arise. With three instruments the predicate becomes a PARAMETER of the question -- the same three data sets are equal or not depending on the tolerance, so the interesting output is not a boolean but the threshold at which agreement appears, which is a measurement about the instruments rather than about the data. In the differential tester list= is buried inside a loop and its boolean is a filter: every input where three implementations disagree gets collected, so the output names the counterexamples rather than reporting a verdict. Same verb; it goes from answering a question, to being swept across a parameter, to being the oracle inside a search for inputs that break something.
row-3-dimension.meta: Rung two varies the equality and holds the data fixed; rung three holds the equality fixed and varies the data. Those are the only two ways to use a parameterised comparison, and each one asks a different kind of question.
row-3-dimension.eng: Instruments do not agree; they agree to a tolerance. Reporting the tolerance at which agreement starts is more useful than reporting a boolean at a tolerance someone guessed.
row-3-dimension.math: A family of equivalence relations indexed by a tolerance is not a nested family -- approximate equality is not transitive -- which is why the threshold is a report and not a proof.
row-3-dimension.cs: Differential testing needs an equality oracle and a supply of inputs. list= is the oracle, and it extends to three implementations without becoming three comparisons.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (reflexive? xs) (list= equal? xs xs))
(define (symmetric? a b) (eq? (list= equal? a b) (list= equal? b a)))
(display (map (lambda (p) (and (reflexive? (car p)) (symmetric? (car p) (cdr p))))
              (list (cons '(1 2) '(1 2)) (cons '(1 2) '(2 1)) (cons '() '())
                    (cons '(a) '()) (cons '(1 (2)) '(1 (2))))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (transitive-holds? a b c)
  (if (and (list= = a b) (list= = b c)) (list= = a c) #t))
(display (map (lambda (t) (apply transitive-holds? t))
              '(((1 2) (1 2) (1 2)) ((1 2) (1 2) (1 3)) ((1) (2) (3))
                (() () ()) ((5 5) (5 5) (5 5)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (matches-pairwise-chain? . ls)
  (let ((direct (apply list= equal? ls)))
    (let loop ((r ls))
      (cond ((or (null? r) (null? (cdr r))) (eq? direct #t))
            ((not (list= equal? (car r) (cadr r))) (eq? direct #f))
            (else (loop (cdr r)))))))
(display (list (matches-pairwise-chain? '(1 2) '(1 2) '(1 2))
               (matches-pairwise-chain? '(1 2) '(1 2) '(9 9))
               (matches-pairwise-chain? '(1 2) '(9 9) '(1 2))
               (matches-pairwise-chain? '(7))
               (matches-pairwise-chain? '() '())))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: Under an equivalence predicate list= is itself an equivalence on lists -- reflexive and symmetric in the first program, transitive in the second -- and the n-list form means exactly the conjunction of the adjacent two-list comparisons, which is what the third program checks against a hand-built chain.
row-4-proof.invariant: For any equivalence e: list=(e, xs, xs) is #t; list=(e, a, b) = list=(e, b, a); list=(e, a, b) and list=(e, b, c) implies list=(e, a, c); and list=(e, l1 ... ln) = the conjunction over i of list=(e, li, li+1)
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: the equivalence laws, and then the reduction of the n-ary form to the binary one. What would falsify them: a list not equal to itself, an asymmetric answer, a transitivity break under an honest equivalence, or an n-list call that disagreed with the chain of pairwise calls -- which is what a buggy short-circuit would look like. The middle chain in the third program mismatches at the FIRST step and the last one at the second step, so both short-circuit positions are covered.
row-4-proof.eng: Reflexivity is what makes list= safe inside a memo or a cache lookup. A comparison that says a value differs from itself corrupts every structure built on it.
row-4-proof.math: An equivalence lifted pointwise over sequences is again an equivalence, provided lengths must match. Dropping the length requirement is exactly what breaks transitivity.
row-4-proof.cs: The n-ary form reducing to a chain of binary comparisons is the contract that lets a caller refactor between the two without changing behavior -- including on the vacuous one-list case.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (same-batch? tol a b) (list= (lambda (x y) (<= (abs (- x y)) tol)) a b))
(define (group-batches tol runs)
  (let loop ((r runs) (groups '()))
    (if (null? r)
        (reverse (map reverse groups))
        (let place ((g groups) (seen '()))
          (cond ((null? g) (loop (cdr r) (cons (list (car r)) (reverse seen))))
                ((same-batch? tol (caar g) (car r))
                 (loop (cdr r) (append (reverse seen) (cons (cons (car r) (car g)) (cdr g)))))
                (else (place (cdr g) (cons (car g) seen))))))))
(display (group-batches 0.1 '((1.0 2.0) (1.05 2.02) (9.0 9.0) (1.0 2.09) (9.02 8.99))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (rows-agree? e rows) (apply list= e rows))
(define (rank-of-agreement rows)
  (let loop ((tol 0) (n 0))
    (if (or (> n 5) (rows-agree? (lambda (a b) (<= (abs (- a b)) tol)) rows))
        (list 'tolerance tol 'agree (rows-agree? (lambda (a b) (<= (abs (- a b)) tol)) rows))
        (loop (+ tol 1) (+ n 1)))))
(display (list 'tight (rank-of-agreement '((10 20) (10 20)))
               'loose (rank-of-agreement '((10 20) (12 19) (11 21)))
               'never (rank-of-agreement '((0 0) (99 99)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (outputs-match? . os) (apply list= equal? os))
(define (property-check f g inputs)
  (let loop ((r inputs) (fails '()) (n 0))
    (if (null? r)
        (list 'checked n 'failures (reverse fails))
        (loop (cdr r)
              (if (outputs-match? (f (car r)) (g (car r))) fails (cons (car r) fails))
              (+ n 1)))))
(define (sorted-twice xs) (sort (sort xs <) <))
(define (sorted-once xs) (sort xs <))
(define (broken xs) (reverse (sort xs <)))
(display (list 'idempotent (property-check sorted-twice sorted-once '((3 1 2) (1) () (5 5 4)))
               'caught (property-check broken sorted-once '((3 1 2) (1) (5 4)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: list= answers whether several sequences agree, under an equality the caller supplies.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: same-batch? is one call; group-batches uses it as the membership test of a clustering loop, so measurement runs sort themselves into groups by a tolerance nobody had to convert into a distance metric. math: rows-agree? is one call; rank-of-agreement sweeps the tolerance upward until it fires, turning a boolean into the smallest tolerance at which several rows can be called the same -- a number that describes the data rather than judging it. cs: outputs-match? is one call; property-check runs two functions over a corpus of inputs and collects every input where they disagree, which is the whole of differential property testing, and the idempotence of sort falls out as a one-line property.
row-5-emergence.meta: Each composition uses the helper as a TEST inside a loop, and the loop is what produces the value: a clustering, a threshold, a list of counterexamples. list= never appears in any of the three answers -- it only decides which branch the loop takes, which is what it means for a predicate to be a component rather than the headline.
row-5-emergence.eng: Clustering by an equality predicate rather than a distance metric is coarser and much easier to justify to whoever has to sign off on the tolerance.
row-5-emergence.math: The least tolerance at which a set of measurements agrees is a summary statistic of their spread, and it is cheap to compute by search when the comparison is already parameterised.
row-5-emergence.cs: Property-based testing needs three things: a property, an oracle, and inputs. Making the oracle a parameterised list comparison means the same harness tests idempotence, commutativity, and round-tripping without modification.
